title: The Fire Salamander's Secret Glow
summary: Fire salamanders are easy to spot in Europe. They are black and yellow, and they give off poison to keep hungry animals away. They live in wet forests, near streams, and in mountains. Losing their homes puts them in danger. Now scientists have found a new surprise. Under an ultraviolet light, fire salamanders glow! The glow is strongest on the yellow underside of their bodies and along their sides. It comes from glands in their skin, and even the liquid from the glands can keep glowing for more than 24 hours after it leaves the body. The glow is green and cyan. Parts of the skin take in ultraviolet light, which people cannot see, and send it back out as light we can see. Fireflies, by contrast, make their own light. Scientists do not yet know why salamanders glow. Maybe the glow helps them find each other or pick a mate. Maybe it makes their warning colors stand out more to predators. Bernat Burriel, the study's first author, says it is fascinating that such a well-studied animal still holds secrets.
why_it_matters: It shows you that even animals you might read about in a nature book can still hide surprises, so staying curious on a walk outside can lead to real discoveries.

keywords.explanation: Ultraviolet is a kind of light that people cannot see with their eyes.
Glands are small parts in skin or a body that make a liquid or substance.
Cyan is a bright blue-green color.
Predators are animals that hunt and eat other animals.
A mate is an animal partner chosen for having babies.

background_read: A fire salamander is a small animal with smooth, damp skin that lives in wet places like forests and near streams.
Its skin has glands that can make substances to protect it from hungry animals.
Some living things give off light, and scientists study glowing skin to learn how animals warn others or find each other.

WHAT: The discovery that fire salamanders glow under an ultraviolet light.
WHERE: In Europe, in wet forests, near streams, and in mountains.
WHY: Scientists want to learn whether the glow helps salamanders find each other, pick a mate, or make their warning colors stand out to predators.
